claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a well-characterized hierarchical heterostructure.
The hierarchical heterostructure contains nanoscale phase dispersions and multiscale grain-boundary networks.
The relevant heterostructure includes grain boundaries, phase interfaces, and precipitate distributions.
The hierarchical heterostructure governs local stress distributions.
The hierarchical heterostructure governs crack-initiation pathways.
Quantitative descriptors of the heterostructure can be extracted from high-resolution imaging and diffraction data.
Encoding these microstructural descriptors in a machine-learning model captures nonlinear correlations between local structural features and macroscopic mechanical responses.
The descriptor-based machine-learning framework reduces reliance on computationally intensive iterative simulations.
The machine-learning framework can predict Young's modulus for HfNbTiVAl10 under tensile testing.
The machine-learning framework can predict yield strength for HfNbTiVAl10 under tensile testing.
The machine-learning framework can predict fracture behavior for HfNbTiVAl10 under fracture testing.
The machine-learning framework will reduce prediction error by at least 10% compared with conventional simulations when predictions are assessed against experiments.
The machine-learning framework will reduce computational prediction time by about 50% compared with conventional simulations.
Insufficient imaging resolution may cause the predictive framework to fail by omitting critical microstructural features.
Nanoscale defects or phase variations outside the training regime may cause the predictive framework to fail.
Very high strain rates or extreme temperatures may activate mechanisms absent from the model and cause prediction failure.
Prediction gains depend on microstructural-data quality and the representativeness of the training set.
